newsitem.title: USA: Flooded Ohio River Valley escapes heaviest rains.
newsitem.headline: Flooded Ohio River Valley escapes heaviest rains.

text.p: Skies cleared Friday along the Ohio River Valley, where flood-weary residents escaped the heaviest rains from a powerful storm that spawned violent weather in the South and dumped snow further North.

"We got kind of lucky," said Chris Jones of the National Weather Service in Paducah, where the Ohio River crested Friday. The river's crest was expected to gradually pass out of the Ohio and into the wider Mississippi River.

Residents along river towns in western Kentucky and southern Illinois have spent several days filling and stacking sandbags to gird against the river's rising waters, which were fed by a deluge two weeks earlier.
The latest batch of storms brought less than an inch (2.5 cm) of rain to areas dealing with floodwaters from the Ohio River and the backed-up creeks and streams that flow into it.
"The additional rainfall shouldn't really do much to the rivers," Jones said.
"The most optimistic people said that the rain was helpful because it washed the mud away," Weather Service hydrologist Michael Callahan said.
The heaviest rainfall fell across Missouri, Alabama, Tennessee and Georgia. At least one tornado struck Columbus, Georgia, damaging homes but causing no serious injuries.
Meanwhile, a snowstorm along the northern tier of Midwestern states merged with the rainstorm spinning out of the South, and dumped snow and sleet on the Northeast.
On the western border of Wisconsin in Lacrosse, schools were closed and roads clogged with a 14-inch (36 cm) snowfall, the state's biggest one-day snowstorm ever in March.
"It was like watching snowballs flying out of the sky," said Angela Williams of the city of 52,000. "It's crappy."
In Detroit, dozens of crews worked to restore electrical service to more than 200,000 customers who lost power during a fierce ice storm.
"The buildup of ice on trees and wires and higher winds expected this afternoon means more power outages are possible," Detroit Edison executive vice president Robert Buckler said.
An Arctic cold wave swept in behind the storm, bringing temperatures as low as minus 16 degrees (minus 27 C) accompanied by high winds.
The return of winter's chill postponed flooding across the Dakotas, where runoff from the huge snowpack was sending rivers and creeks out of their banks.

One novel idea involving sprinkling sand on selected stretches of the iced-over Red River in North Dakota. The Federal Emergency Management Agency said the sand would soak up heat from the sun and melt those sections faster and reduce the damage to bridges from jammed-up ice.
